claim: Bacteriophages were isolated from filter-sterilized wastewater samples from one of three Northeast Ohio Regional Sewer District wastewater treatment plants (Westerly, Southerly, or Easterly Sewage Treatment plant).
source: Bacteriophages were isolated from filter-sterilized wastewater samples from one of three Northeast Ohio Regional Sewer District wastewater treatment plants (Westerly, Southerly, or Easterly Sewage Treatment plant).
evidence: This is a direct statement in the Methods section describing the source of bacteriophage isolation.

claim: Four phages were identified that could form plaques on the ∆fliF ∆pilA double mutant strain, but not the parental wild-type P. aeruginosa PAO1.
source: the screen identified four phages that could form plaques on the ∆fliF ∆pilA double mutant strain, but not the parental wild-type P. aeruginosa PAO1.
evidence: This is a direct observation from the screening experiment described in the Results section.

claim: The four phages isolated were named Clew-1, Clew-3, Clew-6, and Clew-10.
source: We named these Cleveland wastewater-derived phages Clew-1,–3, –6, and –10.
evidence: This is a direct statement about the naming of the isolated phages.

claim: It was the fliF deletion that rendered P. aeruginosa permissive for infection by these phages.
source: Subsequent tests determined that it was the fliF deletion that rendered P. aeruginosa permissive for infection by these phages.
evidence: This is a conclusion drawn from subsequent testing described in the Results section.

claim: All four Clew phage can plaque on a fliF deletion mutant of P. aeruginosa PAO1, but not the corresponding wild-type strain or ∆pilA mutant strain.
source: All four Clew phage can plaque on a fliF deletion mutant of P. aeruginosa PAO1, but not the corresponding wild-type strain or ∆pilA mutant strain (Figure 1A, Figure 1—figure supplement 1A, B, Figure 1—figure supplement 2).
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in multiple figures.

claim: The Clew bacteriophages belong to the family of Bruynogheviruses.
source: The Clew bacteriophages belong to the family of Bruynogheviruses (Lefkowitz et al., 2018) and are all highly related (Figure 1B, Figure 1—figure supplement 1C).
evidence: This is based on phylogenetic analysis shown in Figure 1B and cited literature.

claim: Morphologically, the Clew phages are Podoviruses.
source: Morphologically, like other members of the family, they are Podoviruses (Figure 1C).
evidence: This is based on electron microscopy imaging shown in Figure 1C.

claim: Mutations affecting the MS-ring (∆fliF) and associated proteins FliE or FliG resulted in Clew-1 sensitivity.
source: Mutations affecting the MS-ring (∆fliF) and associated proteins FliE or FliG (Minamino et al., 2020) resulted in Clew-1 sensitivity.
evidence: This is based on experimental testing of various flagellar mutants described in the Results section.

claim: Mutations in the ATPase complex only conferred partial sensitivity to Clew-1.
source: However, mutations in the ATPase complex only conferred partial sensitivity
evidence: This is based on experimental testing of flagellar mutants described in the Results section.

claim: Mutations affecting the hook or flagellar filament did not result in Clew-1 sensitivity.
source: mutations affecting the hook or flagellar filament did not result in sensitivity
evidence: This is based on experimental testing of flagellar mutants described in the Results section.

claim: A mutation that affects the type III secretion function of the flagellar basal body by impeding proton flux, flhA(R147A), did not result in Clew-1 sensitivity.
source: nor did a mutation that affects the type III secretion function of the flagellar basal body by impeding proton flux, flhA(R147A)(Erhardt et al., 2017; Figure 1—figure supplement 4).
evidence: This is based on experimental testing of a specific flagellar mutant.

claim: It is the presence of the MS-ring and not other aspects of the flagellum that controls phage sensitivity.
source: We, therefore, conclude that it is the presence of the MS-ring and not other aspects of the flagellum, such as assembly of the full flagellar structure or flagellar rotation, that controls phage sensitivity.
evidence: This is a conclusion drawn from the experimental data on various flagellar mutants.

claim: Deletion of fleQ had a very minor effect on Clew-1 phage susceptibility of the wild-type bacteria.
source: we found that deletion of fleQ, which is required for transcription of flagellar genes (Arora et al., 1997), had a very minor effect on Clew-1 phage susceptibility of the wild-type bacteria
evidence: This is based on experimental data shown in Figure 1—figure supplement 1E.

claim: Deletion of fleQ decreased Clew-1 susceptibility of the ∆fliF mutant bacteria.
source: and actually decreased Clew-1 susceptibility of the ∆fliF mutant bacteria (Figure 1—figure supplement 1E).
evidence: This is based on experimental data shown in Figure 1—figure supplement 1E.

claim: FleQ is a c-di-GMP-responsive transcription factor that reciprocally controls flagellar gene expression and production of biofilm-related characteristics.
source: FleQ is a c-di-GMP-responsive transcription factor that, among other things, reciprocally controls flagellar gene expression and production of biofilm-related characteristics, such as the production of the extracellular polysaccharides Psl and Pel, as well as the adhesin CdrA (Arora et al., 1997; Oladosu et al., 2024; Dasgupta et al., 2003).
evidence: This is based on cited literature about FleQ function.

claim: Lowering c-di-GMP levels in the ∆fliF2 mutant by producing the c-di-GMP phosphodiesterase PA2133 from a plasmid restored Clew-1 resistance.
source: Lowering c-di-GMP levels in the ∆fliF2 mutant restored Clew-1 resistance (Figure 1D)
evidence: This is based on experimental data shown in Figure 1D.

claim: Deleting wspF rendered the parental PAO1 strain phage sensitive.
source: whereas deleting wspF rendered the parental PAO1 strain phage sensitive (Figure 1E).
evidence: This is based on experimental data shown in Figure 1E.

claim: Clew-1 susceptibility is controlled by intracellular c-di-GMP levels.
source: Taken together, these data demonstrate that Clew-1 susceptibility is controlled by intracellular c-di-GMP levels
evidence: This is a conclusion drawn from the c-di-GMP manipulation experiments.

claim: Absence of the MS-ring controls phage susceptibility through an increase in c-di-GMP.
source: and argue that absence of the MS-ring controls phage susceptibility through an increase in c-di-GMP.
evidence: This is a conclusion drawn from the experimental data on fliF mutants and c-di-GMP manipulation.

claim: A TnSeq experiment in wild-type strain PAO1F infected with phage Clew-1 identified insertion mutants that were depleted after infection.
source: In the first of these, we mutagenized the wild-type strain PAO1F with the mini-mariner transposon TnFAC (Wong and Mekalanos, 2000), and the resultant mutant library was infected with phage Clew-1 at an MOI of 10 for 2 hr. The surviving bacteria were allowed to grow up after plating on an LB plate and the transposon insertion sites for the input and output pools were determined by Illumina sequencing. We identified insertion mutants that were depleted after infection (Figure 2A).
evidence: This is based on TnSeq experimental data shown in Figure 2A.

claim: Two of the genes with the most significant depletion in the wild-type TnSeq experiment were fliF and fliG.
source: Two of the genes with the most significant depletion were fliF and fliG, consistent with our previous analysis indicating that these mutations sensitize PAO1 to Clew-1 infection.
evidence: This is based on TnSeq data analysis shown in Figure 2A.

claim: Depletion of pch and bifA insertions was noted in the wild-type TnSeq experiment.
source: Interestingly, we also noted depletion of pch and bifA insertions, both encoding phosphodiesterases that are involved in depleting c-di-GMP in the flagellated daughter cell after cell division (Kulasekara et al., 2013; Laventie et al., 2019; Manner et al., 2023; Kuchma et al., 2007).
evidence: This is based on TnSeq data analysis and cited literature about pch and bifA function.

claim: Pch interacts with the chemotactic machinery.
source: In fact, pch interacts with the chemotactic machinery (Kulasekara et al., 2013), highlighting, here too, the importance of c-di-GMP in controlling Clew-1 sensitivity.
evidence: This is based on cited literature about pch function.

claim: A TnSeq analysis in a fliF mutant strain identified insertions in the psl operon as the most highly enriched group of mutants after Clew-1 selection.
source: In a reciprocal experiment, we carried out the TnSeq analysis in a fliF mutant strain. This analysis identified insertions in the psl operon as the most highly enriched group of mutants after Clew-1 selection, suggesting that Psl is required for phage infection (Figure 2B).
evidence: This is based on TnSeq experimental data shown in Figure 2B.

claim: Deletion of pslC rendered the fliF mutant bacteria Clew-1 resistant.
source: Deletion of either pslC or pslD rendered the fliF mutant bacteria Clew-1 resistant
evidence: This is based on experimental data shown in Figure 2C.

claim: Deletion of pslD rendered the fliF mutant bacteria Clew-1 resistant.
source: Deletion of either pslC or pslD rendered the fliF mutant bacteria Clew-1 resistant
evidence: This is based on experimental data shown in Figure 2C.

claim: Sensitivity to Clew-1 could be restored through complementation using a plasmid-borne copy of pslC or pslD.
source: and sensitivity could be restored through complementation using a plasmid-borne copy of the deleted open reading frame (Figure 2C).
evidence: This is based on complementation experiments shown in Figure 2C.

claim: PslC is a glycosyltransferase required for Psl biosynthesis.
source: PslC is a glycosyltransferase required for Psl biosynthesis, while PslD is required for Psl export from the cell (Byrd et al., 2009; Wu et al., 2019).
evidence: This is based on cited literature about PslC function.

claim: PslD is required for Psl export from the cell.
source: PslC is a glycosyltransferase required for Psl biosynthesis, while PslD is required for Psl export from the cell (Byrd et al., 2009; Wu et al., 2019).
evidence: This is based on cited literature about PslD function.

claim: Psl production is required for infection of P. aeruginosa by phage Clew-1.
source: These data demonstrate that Psl production is required for infection of P. aeruginosa by phage Clew-1.
evidence: This is a conclusion drawn from the pslC and pslD deletion experiments.

claim: Attachment of phage Clew-1 is Psl-dependent in both wild-type and ∆fliF2 mutant bacteria.
source: Attachment of phage Clew-1 is Psl-dependent. Interestingly, we were able to detect Psl-dependent attachment both with wild-type and ∆fliF2 mutant bacteria (Figure 3A)
evidence: This is based on efficiency of center of infection (ECOI) analysis shown in Figure 3A.

claim: The ∆fliF2 mutant strain was lysed after ~40 min of Clew-1 infection in liquid media.
source: The ∆fliF2 mutant strain was lysed after ~40 min of infection.
evidence: This is based on lysis curve experiments shown in Figure 3—figure supplement 1.

claim: Wild-type bacteria displayed a significant slowing of growth upon Clew-1 infection when compared to the uninfected culture, but not clear lysis as was observed with the ∆fliF2 mutant.
source: The wild-type bacteria displayed a significant slowing of growth upon Clew-1 infection when compared to the uninfected culture, but not clear lysis as was observed with the ∆fliF2 mutant.
evidence: This is based on lysis curve experiments shown in Figure 3—figure supplement 1.

claim: Deleting pslC abolished any phage-dependent effect on growth in both wild-type and ∆fliF2 mutant bacteria.
source: In both instances, deleting pslC abolished any phage-dependent effect on growth.
evidence: This is based on lysis curve experiments shown in Figure 3—figure supplement 1.

claim: There was a statistically significant increase in the percentage of bacteria with attached bacteriophage in the ∆fliF2 mutant bacteria compared to the wild-type.
source: We observed a statistically significant increase in the percentage of bacteria with attached bacteriophage in the ∆fliF2 mutant bacteria compared to the wild-type
evidence: This is based on fluorescence microscopy data shown in Figure 3B and 3C.

claim: The increase in c-di-GMP in the ∆fliF2 mutant increases the fraction of Clew-1 susceptible cells in the population.
source: arguing that the increase in c-di-GMP in the ∆fliF2 mutant increases the fraction of Clew-1 susceptible cells in the population.
evidence: This is a conclusion drawn from the phage attachment microscopy data.

claim: No phage was observed attached to the ∆pslC mutant.
source: As anticipated, no phage was observed attached to the corresponding ∆pslC mutant (Figure 3C, Figure 3—figure supplement 2).
evidence: This is based on fluorescence microscopy data shown in Figure 3C.

claim: Phage Clew-1 can be precipitated from filter-sterilized culture supernatants of a ∆fliF2 mutant using an antibody directed against Psl.
source: We were able to pull down phage Clew-1 in a Psl and antibody-dependent manner with ∆fliF2 ∆pslC culture supernatants serving as a control (Figure 4A).
evidence: This is based on immunoprecipitation experiments shown in Figure 4A.

claim: Some Psl-dependent attachment of Clew-1 to magnetic beads was observed in the absence of antibody.
source: Notably, we observed some Psl-dependent attachment in the absence of antibody, arguing that Psl binds non-specifically to the magnetic beads we used in our experiments.
evidence: This is based on immunoprecipitation experiments shown in Figure 4A.

claim: Including the anti-Psl antibody resulted in a statistically significant increase in Clew-1 precipitation compared to background level of attachment.
source: Including the anti-Psl antibody resulted in a statistically significant increase compared to this background level of attachment (Figure 4A).
evidence: This is based on immunoprecipitation experiments shown in Figure 4A.

claim: Phage Clew-1 can be pulled down using a partially purified fraction of cell-associated Psl in a Psl and antibody-dependent manner.
source: We next repeated the pulldown using a partially purified fraction of cell-associated Psl to repeat the pulldown and again found Psl and antibody-dependent precipitation of phage Clew-1 (Figure 4—figure supplement 1).
evidence: This is based on immunoprecipitation experiments shown in Figure 4—figure supplement 1.

claim: Phage Clew-1 can be pulled down using a biotinylated, affinity-purified preparation of Psl.
source: Finally, we examined phage binding using a biotinylated, affinity-purified preparation of Psl and found that we could pull down the phage using this Psl fraction as well, arguing that Clew-1 binds Psl directly (Figure 4B).
evidence: This is based on pulldown experiments with biotinylated Psl shown in Figure 4B.

claim: Clew-1 binds Psl directly.
source: arguing that Clew-1 binds Psl directly (Figure 4B).
evidence: This is a conclusion drawn from the biotinylated Psl pulldown experiments.

claim: Treatment of day one biofilm with phage Clew-1 resulted in a statistically significant decrease in biofilm mass compared to the biomass present at day 1.
source: Treatment of the day one biofilm with phage Clew-1 resulted in a statistically significant decrease in biofilm mass compared to the biomass present at day 1.
evidence: This is based on static biofilm experiments shown in Figure 5B.

claim: Phage Ocp-2 infection did not result in a reduction in biofilm.
source: Phage Ocp-2 infection, on the other hand, did not result in a reduction in biofilm (Figure 5B).
evidence: This is based on static biofilm experiments shown in Figure 5B.

claim: Phage Clew-1 was not able to reduce a biofilm formed by P. aeruginosa strain PA14, a natural psl mutant.
source: Notably, phage Clew-1 was not able to reduce a biofilm formed by P. aeruginosa strain PA14, a natural psl mutant (Figure 5—figure supplement 1).
evidence: This is based on biofilm experiments with PA14 shown in Figure 5—figure supplement 1.

claim: Phage Clew-1, but not Ocp-2, was able to replicate when grown on biofilm bacteria.
source: Consistent with the reduction in biofilm mass seen in Figure 5B, we found that phage Clew-1, but not Ocp-2, was able to replicate when grown on biofilm bacteria (Figure 5C).
evidence: This is based on phage replication experiments on biofilms shown in Figure 5C.

claim: Clew-1 resulted in a significant reduction in viable CFU in biofilms grown on polystyrene microbeads.
source: Clew-1 resulted in a significant reduction in viable CFU, arguing that phage infection kills biofilm bacteria (Figure 5D).
evidence: This is based on CFU quantification experiments shown in Figure 5D.

claim: Infection with Clew-1 resulted in a significant increase in the fraction of the biofilm volume that is PI-positive, indicating that the biofilm bacteria are dying.
source: Infection with Clew-1 resulted in a significant increase in the fraction of the biofilm volume that is PI-positive, indicating that the biofilm bacteria are dying (Figure 5E).
evidence: This is based on LIVE/DEAD staining and confocal microscopy shown in Figure 5E.

claim: Corneal infections by P. aeruginosa involve the formation of a biofilm.
source: Corneal infections by P. aeruginosa involve the formation of a biofilm (Thanabalasuriar et al., 2019; Zegans et al., 2016).
evidence: This is based on cited literature about P. aeruginosa corneal infections.

claim: A bivalent antibody directed against Psl and the type III secretion needle-tip protein, PcrV, was found to be effective in clearing corneal infections.
source: In fact, a bivalent antibody directed against Psl and the type III secretion needle-tip protein, PcrV, was found to be effective in clearing such corneal infections (Thanabalasuriar et al., 2019).
evidence: This is based on cited literature about antibody treatment of corneal infections.

claim: Multidrug-resistant P. aeruginosa was the cause of a recent outbreak of blinding corneal infections in the USA that was associated with contaminated eye drops.
source: Moreover, multidrug-resistant P. aeruginosa was the cause of a recent outbreak of blinding corneal infections in the USA that was associated with contaminated eye drops (Morelli et al., 2023a; Morelli et al., 2023b).
evidence: This is based on cited literature about a recent outbreak.

claim: Mice infected with PAO1 developed severe corneal disease manifest as corneal opacification in the region of bacterial growth indicated by GFP fluorescence.
source: Mice infected with PAO1 developed severe corneal disease manifest as corneal opacification in the region of bacterial growth indicated by GFP fluorescence (Figure 6B–D).
evidence: This is based on mouse keratitis model experiments shown in Figure 6.

claim: Phage Clew-1 treatment significantly reduced the bacterial burden in a mouse model of P. aeruginosa keratitis.
source: In contrast, phage Clew-1 treatment significantly reduced the bacterial burden, and in some instances, completely eradicated the infection, as measured by GFP fluorescence and CFU (Figure 6D and E).
evidence: This is based on mouse keratitis model experiments shown in Figure 6.

claim: In some instances, phage Clew-1 treatment completely eradicated the infection in the mouse keratitis model.
source: In contrast, phage Clew-1 treatment significantly reduced the bacterial burden, and in some instances, completely eradicated the infection, as measured by GFP fluorescence and CFU (Figure 6D and E).
evidence: This is based on mouse keratitis model experiments shown in Figure 6.

claim: Corneal opacity was reduced by the phage Clew-1 treatment, indicating that inflammation was also starting to resolve.
source: Corneal opacity was similarly reduced by the phage treatment, indicating that inflammation was also starting to resolve (Figure 6B and C).
evidence: This is based on mouse keratitis model experiments shown in Figure 6.

claim: Psl is not a capsular polysaccharide.
source: Psl is not a capsular polysaccharide, so this distinguishes the Clew phages from phages such as KP32 that infect Klebsiella pneumoniae.
evidence: This is a statement distinguishing Psl from capsular polysaccharides.

claim: Klebsiella phages use a capsular depolymerase to break down the capsular polysaccharide.
source: Moreover, these Klebsiella phages use a capsular depolymerase to break down the capsular polysaccharide (Squeglia et al., 2020; Dunstan et al., 2021).
evidence: This is based on cited literature about Klebsiella phages.

claim: Clew-1 has no capsular depolymerase activity.
source: Clew-1, on the other hand, has no such activity (Figure 4—figure supplement 2) arguing that the role of Psl in infection is distinct from that seen in capsule-targeting bacteriophage.
evidence: This is based on experimental data shown in Figure 4—figure supplement 2.

claim: The role of Psl in Clew-1 infection is distinct from that seen in capsule-targeting bacteriophage.
source: arguing that the role of Psl in infection is distinct from that seen in capsule-targeting bacteriophage.
evidence: This is a conclusion drawn from the lack of depolymerase activity in Clew-1.

claim: Phage Clew-1 fails to plaque on wild-type P. aeruginosa PAO1, but forms plaques on a fliF mutant.
source: Phage Clew-1 has the surprising quality that it fails to plaque on wild-type P. aeruginosa PAO1, but forms plaques on a fliF mutant.
evidence: This is a summary of the key observation from the Results section.

claim: The fliF mutation generates a c-di-GMP-dependent signal that up-regulates Psl production.
source: We determined that the fliF mutation generates a c-di-GMP-dependent signal that up-regulates Psl production.
evidence: This is a conclusion drawn from the experimental data on c-di-GMP and Psl.

claim: The fliF mutation increases the fraction of bacteria to which the phage can bind, resulting in efficient lysis in liquid cultures, and plaque formation in top agar.
source: Importantly, it increases the fraction of bacteria to which the phage can bind, resulting in efficient lysis in liquid cultures, and plaque formation in top agar.
evidence: This is a conclusion drawn from the attachment and lysis experiments.

claim: Plaque formation is likely masked in the wild-type bacteria by the fraction of cells that are not phage-susceptible.
source: Plaque formation is likely masked in the wild-type bacteria by the fraction of cells that are not phage-susceptible.
evidence: This is a hypothesis based on the observation that only a fraction of wild-type cells bind phage.

claim: Certain Bruynogheviruses are able to bind to P. aeruginosa PAO1, but not plaque.
source: Notably, certain Bruynogheviruses are able to bind to P. aeruginosa PAO1, but not plaque (Costa et al., 2024).
evidence: This is based on cited literature about other Bruynogheviruses.

claim: Phage Clew-1 has evolved to replicate in P. aeruginosa growing in a biofilm.
source: Taken together, our data suggest that phage Clew-1 has evolved to replicate in P. aeruginosa growing in a biofilm.
evidence: This is a conclusion drawn from the biofilm infection experiments.

claim: Given the prevalence of bacterial biofilms in nature, specialization for biofilm infection makes sense.
source: Given the prevalence of bacterial biofilms in nature, this specialization makes sense.
evidence: This is a logical inference based on the prevalence of biofilms in nature.

claim: We may have underestimated the prevalence of biofilm-tropic bacteriophage since standard isolation techniques using plaque formation of wild-type bacteria would miss phage akin to Clew-1.
source: Moreover, our observation suggests that we may have underestimated the prevalence of biofilm-tropic bacteriophage since standard isolation techniques using plaque formation of wild-type bacteria would miss phage akin to Clew-1.
evidence: This is a conclusion drawn from the observation that Clew-1 does not plaque on wild-type bacteria.

claim: Another bacteriophage was recently described that requires an intact psl operon for replication and can only plaque on PAO1 with elevated c-di-GMP levels.
source: In fact, another bacteriophage was recently described that requires an intact psl operon for replication and can only plaque on PAO1 with elevated c-di-GMP levels (Manner et al., 2023).
evidence: This is based on cited literature about another biofilm-tropic phage.

claim: The bacteriophage Knedl belongs to the family of Iggyviruses.
source: This bacteriophage, Knedl, belongs to the family of Iggyviruses (Maffei et al., 2024), highlighting that more biofilm-tropic bacteriophage wait to be discovered.
evidence: This is based on cited literature about the Knedl phage.

claim: More biofilm-tropic bacteriophage wait to be discovered.
source: highlighting that more biofilm-tropic bacteriophage wait to be discovered.
evidence: This is a conclusion drawn from the discovery of multiple biofilm-tropic phages.

claim: Using a ∆fliF ∆pilA double mutant will allow enrichment for biofilm-specific bacteriophage, by excluding dominant type IV pilus-dependent phage and up-regulating biofilm-specific surface structures such as Psl, Pel, and CdrA.
source: Our data also suggest that, for P. aeruginosa, using a ∆fliF ∆pilA double mutant will allow us to enrich for biofilm-specific bacteriophage, by excluding dominant type IV pilus-dependent phage and up-regulating biofilm-specific surface structures such as Psl, Pel, and CdrA.
evidence: This is a conclusion drawn from the experimental approach used to isolate Clew-1.

claim: Treatment modalities that are targeted towards biofilm bacteria are sorely needed given the importance of biofilms in contributing to the antibiotic resistance of P. aeruginosa in infections.
source: Given the importance of biofilms in contributing to the antibiotic resistance of P. aeruginosa in infections such as the CF lung, catheters, or wound infections, treatment modalities that are targeted towards biofilm bacteria are sorely needed.
evidence: This is a statement about the clinical need for biofilm-targeting therapies.

claim: Phage Clew-1 shows some promise as a treatment modality since it was able to kill biofilm bacteria in vitro, and control P. aeruginosa infection in a mouse model of keratitis.
source: Indeed, phage Clew-1 shows some promise in this regard, since it was able to kill biofilm bacteria in vitro, and control P. aeruginosa infection in a mouse model of keratitis, which involves biofilm formation at the site of infection.
evidence: This is a conclusion drawn from the in vitro and in vivo experimental data.

claim: Clew-1 plaques can sometimes look turbid, which is likely a function of the fact that Clew-1 can only bind to a fraction of the bacterial population.
source: While Clew-1 plaques can sometimes look turbid, this is likely a function of the fact that Clew-1 can only bind to a fraction of the bacterial population (80–90% in the case of PAO1 ∆fliF2, Figure 3).
evidence: This is an explanation for the turbid plaque phenotype based on attachment data.

claim: We have not been able to isolate Clew-1 lysogens.
source: We have not been able to isolate Clew-1 lysogens
evidence: This is a statement about unsuccessful attempts to isolate lysogens.

claim: The inability to isolate Clew-1 lysogens is consistent with observations using other Bruynogheviruses.
source: which is consistent with observations using other Bruynogheviruses (Knezevic et al., 2021; Ceyssens et al., 2008; Alvi et al., 2021)
evidence: This is based on cited literature about other Bruynogheviruses.

claim: Clew-1 is lytic and not temperate.
source: and argues that Clew-1 is lytic and not temperate.
evidence: This is a conclusion drawn from the inability to isolate lysogens.

claim: Many bacteriophages are not able to infect P. aeruginosa biofilms.
source: While many bacteriophages are not able to infect P. aeruginosa biofilms, some phages with the ability to target biofilms have been described, including the Bruynoghevirus Delta (Knezevic et al., 2021).
evidence: This is based on cited literature about phage-biofilm interactions.

claim: Some phages with the ability to target P. aeruginosa biofilms have been described, including the Bruynoghevirus Delta.
source: some phages with the ability to target biofilms have been described, including the Bruynoghevirus Delta (Knezevic et al., 2021).
evidence: This is based on cited literature about biofilm-targeting phages.

claim: Capsule-targeting bacteriophages tend to use LPS as a secondary receptor for tight binding to the target cell.
source: Capsule-targeting bacteriophages tend to use LPS as a secondary receptor for tight binding to the target cell.
evidence: This is a statement about the general behavior of capsule-targeting phages.

claim: Clew-1 does not seem to require either A- or B-band LPS for infection.
source: While Clew-1 does not seem to require either A- or B-band LPS for infection (Figure 1—figure supplement 3)
evidence: This is based on experimental data shown in Figure 1—figure supplement 3.

claim: Several genes involved in the biosynthesis of outer core LPS were hit in the TnSeq analysis.
source: we did hit several genes involved in the biosynthesis of outer core LPS in our TnSeq analysis (Supplementary file 3).
evidence: This is based on TnSeq data analysis.

claim: The gene ssg (PA5001) is required for Clew-1 infection.
source: We tested whether one of these genes, ssg (PA5001), is required for Clew-1 infection and found that this is the case (Figure 1—figure supplement 3).
evidence: This is based on experimental testing shown in Figure 1—figure supplement 3.

claim: It has been noted previously that flagellar mutations lead to increases in c-di-GMP levels and increased production of Psl upon surface contact.
source: While it has been noted previously that flagellar mutations lead to increases in c-di-GMP levels and increased production of Psl upon surface contact (Harrison et al., 2020)
evidence: This is based on cited literature about flagellar mutations and c-di-GMP.

claim: Phage susceptibility was primarily the result of loss of the MS-ring and associated proteins (FliEFG), not the flagellar filament (FliC).
source: our results differ somewhat in that phage susceptibility was primarily the result of loss of the MS-ring and associated proteins (FliEFG), not, for example, the flagellar filament (FliC).
evidence: This is a conclusion drawn from the flagellar mutant analysis.

claim: The difference in phage susceptibility between MS-ring and filament mutants may be due to differences between planktonically grown and surface-attached bacteria.
source: This may be due to differences between planktonically grown (as in our study) and surface-attached bacteria.
evidence: This is a hypothesis to explain the observed differences.

claim: Surface contact leads to up-regulation of c-di-GMP through surface sensing by the Wsp chemosensory system.
source: Surface contact leads to up-regulation of c-di-GMP through surface sensing by the Wsp chemosensory system (Hickman et al., 2005; Armbruster et al., 2019).
evidence: This is based on cited literature about surface sensing and c-di-GMP.

claim: Attached bacteria divide asymmetrically, with c-di-GMP levels decreasing in the flagellated daughter cell.
source: Attached bacteria divide asymmetrically, with c-di-GMP levels decreasing in the flagellated daughter cell (Kulasekara et al., 2013; Laventie et al., 2019; Manner et al., 2023; Christen et al., 2010).
evidence: This is based on cited literature about asymmetric cell division and c-di-GMP.

claim: The asymmetry in c-di-GMP levels requires the phosphodiesterase Pch, which has been reported to bind to the chemosensory protein CheA.
source: This asymmetry requires the phosphodiesterase Pch, which has been reported to bind to the chemosensory protein CheA (Kulasekara et al., 2013; Laventie et al., 2019).
evidence: This is based on cited literature about Pch function.

claim: A second phosphodiesterase, BifA, is also required for maintaining c-di-GMP homeostasis and developing an asymmetric program of cell division upon attachment to surfaces.
source: A second phosphodiesterase, BifA, is also required for maintaining c-di-GMP homeostasis and developing an asymmetric program of cell division upon attachment to surfaces (Manner et al., 2023; Kuchma et al., 2007).
evidence: This is based on cited literature about BifA function.

claim: In the TnSeq experiment, insertions in flagellar genes, such as fliF and fliG, but also insertions in pch and bifA resulted in Clew-1 sensitivity.
source: In our TnSeq experiment, we found that insertions in flagellar genes, such as fliF and fliG, but also insertions in pch and bifA resulted in Clew-1 sensitivity.
evidence: This is based on TnSeq data analysis.

claim: Phages such as Clew-1 or Knedl could be a useful tool for interrogating c-di-GMP signaling pathways in P. aeruginosa.
